subject: psychiatry
title: Delirium

steps.tx: **Delirium** disturbs attention and awareness acutely over hours to days with fluctuating cognition from a medical cause that the team must find urgently. Dementia instead progresses over years with attention preserved early, although delirium superimposed on dementia fills most hospital wards today. **Hypoactive delirium** stays quiet, withdrawn and drowsy, gets missed most often and carries the worst outcomes of any motor subtype. Infection, hypoxia, metabolic upset, drugs, withdrawal, pain and retention all belong on the first checklist.
steps.say: Delirium arrives over hours and attention fails while awareness fluctuates through the day. Dementia is a slow disorder over years and attention is preserved early in that slower course of decline. Quiet delirium gets missed most and those patients fare worst on wards. Every case needs a medical search because infection and drug effects commonly drive the acute presentation in hospital.

steps.tx: The flowchart applies **Confusion Assessment Method** logic, which needs an acute fluctuating course plus inattention, and then either disorganised thinking or altered consciousness to confirm delirium. Family history establishes the baseline and proves acuity, while examination hunts infection source, dehydration and drug culprits such as anticholinergics, opioids and benzodiazepines. Observations, glucose, bloods, cultures and ECG follow the clues, and imaging waits for focal signs, trauma or failure to improve. **Collateral history** therefore matters as much as any scan.
steps.say: Diagnosis needs acute change first and inattention must accompany that fluctuating course clearly. Disorganised thinking completes the method or altered consciousness satisfies the final branch instead. Family members prove baseline best and drug charts reveal culprits during review rounds. Imaging waits for focal signs because most causes appear in bloods first.

steps.tx: **Multicomponent prevention** with orientation, hydration, early mobilisation, sleep hygiene, glasses, hearing aids and pain control prevents about a third of hospital delirium cases. Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium generally and stay reserved at low dose for severe distress or danger that de-escalation cannot contain safely. Benzodiazepines worsen delirium except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, where they become the treatment itself for the underlying cause. Restraints and catheters aggravate confusion, and **Lewy body disease** makes antipsychotic sensitivity potentially lethal.
steps.say: Prevention works through simple care and orientation with hydration prevents many hospital cases. Glasses restore vision well and hearing aids restore communication during ward rounds daily. Antipsychotics help danger only and routine sedation prolongs confusion in most patients unfortunately. Benzodiazepines worsen delirium generally although withdrawal delirium needs them as treatment.

steps.tx: This ward room assembles **delirium prevention** at one bedside, with a clock and calendar for orientation, water for hydration, and glasses with a hearing aid case within easy reach. A nurse helps the patient sit up beside a walker, which shows **early mobilisation**, while daylight through the window supports sleep hygiene at night. None of these items is a drug, yet together they prevent about a third of hospital cases. For the exam, you should list the bundle before reaching for sedation.
steps.say: The room is arranged for prevention clearly and a clock with a calendar helps orientation for the patient at bedside. Water prevents dehydration daily and glasses with hearing aids restore sensory input well. A walker encourages mobilisation early and daylight supports healthy sleep at night. Together these simple measures prevent many cases without any sedative drug.

steps.tx: **Prognosis after delirium** extends beyond the ward, because episodes multiply mortality, institutional care and **later dementia** risk in older survivors for years. Discharge therefore needs cognitive follow up with family explanation that recovery may take weeks to months after the infection clears. Persistent delirium demands a fresh hunt for occult infection, subdural bleeding, autoimmune disease or non convulsive seizures with EEG support. Capacity fluctuates with delirium, so major decisions wait for clearer days or use legal frameworks with reassessment.
steps.say: Delirium scars recovery long term and mortality rises after discharge from hospital wards. Cognitive follow up matters greatly because dementia risk climbs in survivors afterwards persistently. Persistent confusion needs reinvestigation always and EEG detects silent seizures in some patients. Decisions wait for lucidity where possible because capacity fluctuates with delirium.
